title: Lumbini Travel Guide: Sites, Fees, Timings and Tips
meta_description: Lumbini travel guide: how to reach, Maya Devi Temple fees and timings, monastic zone, where to stay, how many days, costs and tips for Indian and foreign visitors.
summary: Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace, lies 22 km west of Bhairahawa and 26 km from the Sonauli border. Fly from Kathmandu in 35 minutes or drive 8–10 hours. Allow two nights: the Maya Devi Temple at dawn, the monastic zone by bicycle and a half-day at Tilaurakot. October to March is the comfortable season.

sections.heading: Lumbini at a glance
paras: Lumbini is a small town and a large protected site on the Terai plain of Rupandehi district, at about 150 m above sea level. Buddhist tradition holds that Siddhartha Gautama was born here around 563 BCE while his mother, Queen Maya Devi, was travelling from Kapilavastu to her family home at Devdaha. Emperor Ashoka visited about 249 BCE and raised an inscribed pillar that names the spot as the Buddha's birthplace. UNESCO listed Lumbini as a World Heritage Site in 1997.

The protected area follows a master plan by Japanese architect Kenzo Tange: a rectangle about 4.8 km long and 1.6 km wide. In the south is the Sacred Garden with the Maya Devi Temple. A long canal runs north through the Monastic Zone, where Buddhist countries have built temples in their own styles, to the Lumbini Museum, the research institute and New Lumbini Village at the northern end. Hotels and the small bazaar sit around the edges.

sections.heading: How to reach Lumbini
paras: By air, fly from Kathmandu to Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa. Buddha Air, Yeti Airlines and Shree Airlines usually run several flights a day of about 35 minutes. From the airport it is 30–40 minutes by car to the Lumbini hotels. Indian nationals pay a rupee fare, while other foreign nationals pay a higher dollar fare.

By road from Kathmandu, the route runs via Mugling, Narayanghat and Butwal, about 300 km and 8–10 hours depending on highway works. From Pokhara it is about 210 km and 7–8 hours via the Siddhartha Highway; from Chitwan about 180 km and five hours. Tourist buses serve Bhairahawa from both cities.

From India, most visitors cross at Sonauli–Belahiya, 26 km from Lumbini. Gorakhpur, the nearest major railway junction, is about three hours from the border. Indian citizens need a passport or voter ID; other nationals need a passport and a Nepal visa, which is issued on arrival at Belahiya. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: What to see in the Sacred Garden
paras: The Sacred Garden is the heart of Lumbini and the one place every visitor should see at an unhurried pace. The Maya Devi Temple, a plain white building opened in 2003, protects brick foundations going back to the 3rd century BCE. Inside, a boardwalk leads to the marker stone, found in 1996 and kept under glass, which archaeologists associate with the exact birth spot. A worn stone relief shows Maya Devi holding a branch during the birth. Photography is not allowed inside, and shoes come off at the door.

Beside the temple stands Ashoka's pillar, whose Brahmi inscription states that the Buddha Shakyamuni was born here and that the village was granted a tax reduction. South of the temple is the Puskarini, the brick-lined pond where tradition says Maya Devi bathed. A bodhi tree hung with prayer flags shades the bank, and monks often chant there at dawn. Around them lie the excavated foundations of stupas and monasteries built over many centuries.

sections.heading: Entry fees and opening hours
paras: Entry to the Sacred Garden is charged as a conservation fee by the Lumbini Development Trust, with rates by nationality. Reports from 2026, after a fee revision, put it at about NPR 20 for Nepali citizens, NPR 80 for Indian citizens, NPR 700 for SAARC and Myanmar nationals and NPR 1,000 for other foreigners. Tickets are sold at the gate, by QR payment and through the trust's online ticketing site. The monastic zone itself is free, though individual temples welcome donations.

The Sacred Garden opens early, around 6 am, and closes around sunset, with slightly different hours in summer and winter. Monastery shrine rooms usually open from morning to late afternoon and may close briefly at lunchtime. Fees and hours change, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: How many days to spend
paras: One full day covers the essentials if you start at dawn in the Sacred Garden and cycle the monasteries in the late afternoon. Two nights are better: they add a half-day to Tilaurakot, the ruins of ancient Kapilavastu 27 km west, and give you a second dawn for quiet reflection or the crane wetlands. Pilgrims who also want Kudan, Niglihawa, Ramagrama and Devdaha need four to five nights based in Lumbini.

Lumbini also fits neatly into wider routes. From the Indian side, many families spend one night here on the way to Pokhara and Kathmandu. Travellers heading north can break the long drive to Pokhara with a night in the hill town of Tansen, 90 km away.

sections.heading: Where to stay and what it costs
paras: Lumbini's comfortable hotels are mostly in the 3-star range. Buddha Maya Gardens, run by the KGH Group, sits about five minutes' walk from the Sacred Garden and suits families and pilgrim groups. Lumbini Hokke Hotel offers Japanese-style tatami rooms near the monastic zone. Lumbini Bazaar at the eastern gate has budget guesthouses. Bhairahawa, 20 km away, has more choice, including Hotel Nirvana, for late arrivals or early border crossings.

As a guide to budgets, our 2-night Lumbini pilgrimage with a 3-star hotel, breakfast and dinner, private car, guide and entry fees starts at about ₹14,000 per person for Indian nationals. Bicycles cost a few hundred rupees a day, battery rickshaws about NPR 1,500–2,500 for a half-day, and a full-day car to the Kapilavastu sites around ₹6,500.

sections.heading: Practical tips for a smooth visit
paras: Lumbini is hot for much of the year, so plan sightseeing around the sun. Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, and wear shoes you can slip off at every shrine. Carry water, a hat and sunscreen; in winter, bring socks for cold temple floors and a warm layer for foggy mornings. Indian rupees are widely accepted at a fixed rate of about NPR 1.6 per INR, and ATMs are available in Bhairahawa and a few in Lumbini Bazaar.

Respect is expected at all sites: walk clockwise around stupas, do not point your feet at Buddha images, ask before photographing monks, and keep voices low in the Sacred Garden. Hire bicycles or battery rickshaws for the monastic zone rather than trying to walk it, as the distances are greater than they look on a map.

faqs.a: Yes. Lumbini is the birthplace of the Buddha, confirmed by Ashoka's 3rd-century BCE inscription, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Maya Devi Temple, the pillar, the sacred pond and the international monastic zone make it rewarding for pilgrims and general travellers. Plan at least one full day, ideally two nights.

faqs.q: How do I get to Lumbini from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Fly to Bhairahawa in about 35 minutes, then drive 30–40 minutes to Lumbini. By road, it is about 300 km and 8–10 hours via Mugling, Narayanghat and Butwal, by private car or tourist bus. Flying saves a day; the road allows stops in Chitwan.

faqs.q: What are the Maya Devi Temple timings?
faqs.a: The Sacred Garden, which contains the Maya Devi Temple, opens around 6 am and closes around sunset, with seasonal variation. Dawn is the best time to visit, when monks chant and the air is cool. Hours can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is the Lumbini entry fee for Indians?
faqs.a: Reports after the 2026 revision put the Lumbini Development Trust fee at about NPR 80 for Indian citizens, compared with about NPR 700 for SAARC and Myanmar nationals and NPR 1,000 for other foreigners. Tickets are sold at the gate or online. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I visit Lumbini in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. Visit the Sacred Garden at dawn, rest in the midday heat and cycle the monastic zone from about 3 pm, ending at the World Peace Pagoda. You will miss Tilaurakot and the other Kapilavastu sites, which need a further half-day or day.

faqs.q: What is the best way to get around Lumbini?
faqs.a: Bicycles are the most popular way to cover the 4.8 km master-plan area and are hired in Lumbini Bazaar or at hotels. Battery rickshaws suit seniors and families with young children. Private cars are restricted in parts of the site and are mainly useful for trips to Tilaurakot and other outlying sites.

Yes, Lumbini is generally calm and safe. Take normal care with valuables, use pre-booked transport from the border or airport, and avoid unlit roads at night. The main risks are heat, dehydration and mosquitoes, so carry water, sun protection and repellent.

faqs.q: What should I wear in Lumbini?
faqs.a: Loose, light clothing that covers shoulders and knees, and shoes that slip off easily for temples. A hat, sunglasses and sunscreen are essential from March to June. In December and January, bring a warm layer and socks for cold mornings and temple floors.

There are a few ATMs in Lumbini Bazaar, but they can run out of cash or reject foreign cards. Bhairahawa, 22 km away, has many more banks and ATMs. Indian rupees are accepted widely. Carry enough cash for entry fees, bicycle hire and donations.
